newsitem.title: UK: Rate rise/tax cut seen as wrong mix for UK economy.
newsitem.headline: Rate rise/tax cut seen as wrong mix for UK economy.

text.p: A policy mix of higher interest rates combined with likely tax cuts in the November budget is wrong for the consumer-led British economic recovery, analysts said on Thursday.
Rapidly improving household finances and healthy spending are unlikely to be damaged by Wednesday's surprise quarter-point interest rate rise.
But Britain's struggling manufacturers are. They are largely dependent on overseas markets and could soon find higher rates and a stronger pound are putting the brakes on demand.
"Having hit the sector which least needs hitting, Clarke will probably soon stimulate the sector which least needs stimulating," said Michael Dicks, UK economist at Lehman Brothers.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke is still playing down expectations ahead of the budget but he is under intense pressure from party and cabinet colleagues to deliver a headline-grabbing income tax cut on budget day, November 26.
A general election must be held by May 1997 and the latest opinion polls suggest the opposition Labour Party's lead had widened to 28 points.
On Wednesday, Clarke said he was raising rates to keep a firm grip on inflation.
But since consumers pose the main threat to the tough 2.5 percent inflation target, economists said measures aimed more directly at their pockets would be more effective.

"If the Chancellor is worried that consumer spending is growing too quickly, he should be doing something which has a direct impact on consumers, and the best thing to do is take some of their income away by raising taxes," said David Walton, UK economist at Goldman Sachs.
Raising interest rates would help rein back spending but only in an indirect way, Walton said.

And since most major mortgage lenders said on Wednesday they had no plans to raise their mortage rates and would review the situation after the budget, consumers may not feel any immediate pinch at all.

Consumer spending has grown rapidly, rising 2.3 percent in the year to the second quarter, and is expected to grow even faster next year. The Treasury forecasts a rise of 4.0 percent in 1997 and many economists said even this might be too cautious.
Lower income taxes and mortgage costs, along with higher wages, are largely responsible for lively consumer activity.

But other special factors are at work, too, and their impact is more difficult to assess. In particular, the full effect on spending of a huge flow of cash from maturing tax-exempt investments (TESSAs) and windfall payments from building society mergers and flotations can only be guessed.
Clarke said the rate rise had "nothing to do with the budget" and re-iterated his aim to balance the budget over the medium term. But economists were not convinced.
"If he wasn't intending to cut tax in November, he would have left rates on hold," said Walton.
The policy mix also presents problems for public finances, which remain further in the red than the government would like.

The public sector borrowing requirement continues to overshoot projections and in the summer the Treasury was forced to revise up the estimate for borrowing in 1996/97 to 27 billion pounds ($44 billion) from 22.5 billion.
"In an ideal world, fiscal policy would be tighter and monetary policy relatively loose," said Philip Shaw, group economist at Union Plc. But he was comforted by the rate rise.

"It is reassuring that Clarke has been willing to tighten monetary policy. A fiscal tightening would be preferable but at least the overall policy stance is moving in the right direction for the economic conditions." ($1=.6141 Pound)
